The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2026-03-11.10.1) introduced by Kooyong MP [Monique Ryan](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/kooyong/monique_ryan) (Independent), which means they failed. Dr Ryan [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2026-03-11.10.1): > *This bill seeks to introduce significant changes to Australia's migration regime. It empowers the minister to suspend classes of temporary visas held by people offshore through so-called arrival control determinations. This is a sweeping power, one which could affect thousands of people who have already followed our migration rules in good faith and who have already obtained temporary visas in good faith. The amendments I have circulated in my name seek to strengthen the test for making these arrival control determinations to ensure that the minister will satisfy a higher and more proportionate threshold before exercising this extraordinary power. My amendments will ensure that determinations meet both limbs of the test under section 84B, ensuring that there is a reasonable probability that a controlled determination is actually necessary.* ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, item 6, page 4 (line 23), omit "one or".* > > *(2) Schedule 1, item 6, page 4 (line 25), omit "may", substitute "would".* > > *(3) Schedule 1, item 6, page 4 (line 31), omit "may", substitute "would".*

Moved the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill 2026 to establish time-limited arrival control determinations for certain temporary visa holders outside Australia during overseas events, with safeguards, exemptions, parliamentary reporting and a maximum six-month period; the bill received a second reading and coalition support.

Moved that the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee hold a public hearing from 5 pm to 6.30 pm to hear Department of Home Affairs officials about the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill 2026; the question was agreed to.

Moved amendments to the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill to narrow arrival-control powers, restore parliamentary disallowance, define triggering events, expand family exemptions, require consideration of permitted-travel applications and extend visas after suspension. The government opposed them, arguing the bill's safeguards and risk-based approach were appropriate; the amendments were put to the question.

Presented the Selection of Bills Committee's third report of 2026, which made no recommendations to refer bills to committees, deferred consideration of the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Amendment (Consideration of UNDRIP) Bill 2023, and debated whether the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill 2026 should be referred for inquiry and report by 27 June 2026.

Moved to allocate 45 minutes for the Royal Commissions Legislation Amendment (Protections for Providing Information) Bill 2026 and 1 hour and 15 minutes for the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill 2026, with remaining stages to be put after the allotted times and divisions permitted after 4.30 pm.

Argued that the bill appropriately enables temporary suspension of certain offshore temporary visas following significant international events, with exclusions and ministerial exceptions, and said the coalition would support it. Raised questions about the government's timing, risk assessments and treatment of visa holders from conflict-affected regions, including 6,957 Palestinian nationals and 7,200 people from Iran.

Argued that the Migration Amendment (2026 Measures No. 1) Bill 2026 was rushed and would grant excessive ministerial powers over temporary visa travel, calling for scrutiny, safeguards, natural justice, family protections, compensation and parliamentary disallowance; opposed the bill and foreshadowed amendments.
